analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-run public health plan anyone can buy and boosts health coverage subsidies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in three House committees until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a government-run 'Medicare Part E' health plan that any U.S. resident could buy on their own, through a small or large employer, or on the ACA exchanges. It would cover gold-level benefits, including reproductive services regardless of state bans, and doctors already in Medicare would be in network automatically, with pay rates capped below what commercial insurers pay. It would also cap out-of-pocket costs for regular Medicare beneficiaries at $6,700 a year, raise ACA premium subsidies and extend them permanently, reduce deductibles for lower-income enrollees, put $30 billion into a state reinsurance fund, and strengthen federal review of insurance rates.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and marketplace enrollees, who would get a gold-level public plan with richer subsidies and lower deductibles; workers stuck with unaffordable employer plans, who would gain a voluntary employer option with job-loss portability; and Medicare beneficiaries, who would gain a $6,700 annual cap on out-of-pocket costs for hospital and doctor services [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured, marketplace enrollees, and Medicare beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Establishes Medicare Part E public health plans available in the individual, small group, and large group markets, open to any U.S. resident not already on Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP [S2].
Each plan must cover gold-level benefits plus all Medicare-covered services and all reproductive services, and states cannot block that coverage [S2].
Employers could voluntarily offer the plan, the federal government could administer it, and workers could keep it if they lose their job [S2].
Caps out-of-pocket cost-sharing for Medicare beneficiaries at $6,700 starting in 2026, adjusted to medical inflation thereafter [S2].

Changes ACA premium credits to be calculated against a gold-level benchmark plan, permanently removes the 400% of poverty income cap on eligibility, and expands cost-sharing reductions so lower-income enrollees get plans covering 80-94% of costs [S2].

Appropriates $2 billion in startup funds and $30 billion for fiscal years 2025-2027 for a state reinsurance and affordability fund, plus money for ACA navigator programs; employers who do not offer affordable coverage must refer full-time workers to exchange navigators [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a new government-run competitor paying doctors above Medicare rates but below commercial averages; drug makers would face Medicare-style price negotiation; hospital systems would take lower reimbursement on the plan's business; and taxpayers would fund the $2 billion startup, $30 billion reinsurance fund, and permanent subsidy expansion [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, drug makers, hospitals, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $2 billion in startup funding, unspecified initial reserve funds, and $30 billion for a 2025-2027 state reinsurance fund, on top of permanently extending enhanced premium subsidies to households above 400% of the poverty line, a large ongoing federal cost [S2].

Half of the reinsurance money would flow to private insurance companies as payments for high-cost enrollees, which supporters argue lowers premiums but which also subsidizes the industry directly [S2].

A government plan priced below commercial rates could draw employers and enrollees away from private coverage, the objection insurers and provider groups have historically raised to public-option proposals; hospitals in particular would face reimbursement capped below commercial averages on that business [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a genuine public coverage competitor with major subsidy increases and a real out-of-pocket cap for Medicare beneficiaries. The main costs are fiscal: about $32 billion in appropriations plus an open-ended permanent subsidy expansion, and some of the affordability money reaches consumers only by passing through private insurers first. Provider payment rates below commercial levels are the main design tension, since they hold premiums down but squeeze hospitals and doctors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and twice to a health subcommittee, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so it died without anyone voting on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Jimmy Gomez introduced the Choose Medicare Act on May 1, 2024, with three cosponsors: Reps. Donald Beyer, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jared Huffman [S1].

The bill was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means committees, and on May 3 and December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health [S4].
No committee reported the bill and no vote was ever scheduled in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, drug makers, and hospital systems that would have competed against or been paid less by a new government-run plan are better off, because that plan never came into being. Medicare beneficiaries and marketplace enrollees also did not get the out-of-pocket cap and richer subsidies the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, drug makers, and hospital systems

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican chairs of the three committees it was sent to never scheduled any action on it.

industries.note: A government-run gold-level plan would compete directly with private insurers in the individual, small group, and large group markets, while the bill also sends $30 billion in reinsurance payments to insurers. Insurers gain the payments but lose market share to the public plan, which is why the industry has historically opposed public-option proposals [S2].
The bill applies Medicare's drug price negotiation provisions to Part E plans and extends the excise tax penalty for noncompliance with negotiation requirements to those drugs [S2].

Every provider already participating in Medicare becomes a participating provider automatically, and reimbursement is capped between Medicare rates and commercial averages, with Medicare's balance-billing limits applying. Providers gain a new pool of insured patients but take lower rates on the plan's business [S2].

Employers in any size market could voluntarily offer the public plan, with the government acting as administrator, and workers could keep the coverage after losing a job. This gives employers a cheaper coverage option, though employers offering unaffordable plans face a new obligation to refer workers to exchange navigators [S2].
